claims.text: A model incorporating quantitative atomic-scale disorder metrics will identify low-phonon-thermal-conductivity high-entropy alloys more accurately than current methods.
Severe local structural heterogeneity enhances phonon scattering.
The relevant as-synthesized high-entropy alloys are largely disordered.
Refractory and FCC high-entropy alloys are candidate material classes for the proposed approach.
The predictive algorithm will integrate atomic-size mismatch, composition-derived mixing entropy, simulated vibrational density of states, and experimental scattering data.
Phonon-mediated heat conduction is dominant under the proposed moderate- to high-temperature thermal-insulation conditions.
The approach applies to compositionally complex alloys having minimal electronic thermal conductivity.
Compositional complexity increases lattice distortion.
Compositional complexity increases point-defect density.
Lattice distortion and point defects enhance phonon scattering.
Enhanced atomic-level disorder reduces phonon mean free paths.
Reduced phonon mean free paths lower phonon thermal conductivity.
Accurately quantifying disorder parameters will improve identification of low-phonon-thermal-conductivity alloys.
The proposed model may improve predictive performance by approximately 10–20% over current methods.
Current predictive approaches rely on averaged material properties.
Failure to capture local disorder makes current thermal-conductivity predictions less precise.
The approach is expected to be robust when atomic-scale disorder is the dominant source of phonon scattering.
The approach may have limited applicability when grain-boundary scattering or electronic heat conduction dominates.
The benchmark will compare measured phonon thermal conductivity against predictions from both the proposed model and conventional averaged-property methods.

The hypothesis is falsified if the model fails to outperform conventional methods for at least 80% of tested compositions or if disorder metrics lack a statistically significant correlation with measured thermal conductivity.
